h1: The 6 Best 4K Webcams of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: six true 4K webcams compared on sensor, frame rate, low-light handling, mounting and software support for streamers.
summary: The Logitech MX Brio is the best 4K webcam here, combining true 4K capture, auto light correction, a privacy shutter and a USB-C cable. The Razer Kiyo Pro Ultra wins in dim rooms with a large sensor, and the Elgato Facecam Pro is the only 60 frames per second option. The EMEET C960 is the cheapest way in.
intro: Most video calls compress your picture down to 720p or 1080p before it reaches the other side, so a 4K webcam only pays off when you record or stream locally. Buying one for Zoom alone is the classic mistake, and a good 1080p camera would look just as sharp there. What 4K really buys is cropping room and cleaner detail in a recording.

We reviewed eight webcams and ranked the six that deliver true 4K, judging sensor, frame rate, light handling, mounting and software support from the spec sheets. We did not capture sample footage, so the ranking weighs documented features. Treat sensor size and manual controls as the real differences, because resolution is where every camera here looks the same on paper.

products.name: Logitech MX Brio Ultra HD 4K Webcam (Graphite)
products.verdict: True 4K, auto light correction and a USB-C cable.
products.description:
The MX Brio captures true 4K UHD, corrects lighting automatically, carries a built-in privacy shutter and connects over USB-C. Auto light correction matters more than resolution on a real desk: a webcam that handles a window behind you or a desk lamp beside you will look better than a sharper one that blows out highlights. The wide diagonal field of view also fits shared desks.

It ranks first because it joins 4K to a modern connector and a physical shutter at $100 to $200. The older Brio needs USB 3.0 for full resolution and lists no shutter. The Razer beats it on sensor size and manual control, but costs a full band more and demands tuning.

Buy it if you record content and take calls. The caveat is control: no manual exposure options are listed, so you live with its automatic decisions.

products.name: Razer Kiyo Pro Ultra 4K Webcam
products.verdict: A large sensor and DSLR-style manual controls.
products.description:
The Kiyo Pro Ultra pairs 4K with a large sensor, auto light correction, a built-in mic and shutter, and DSLR-style manual controls. Sensor size is the spec that decides low-light quality. A larger sensor gathers more light per pixel, so footage stays cleaner when you shoot in a dim room without lighting.

It ranks second because it has the best low-light hardware in this roundup but costs $200 to $500, a band above the MX Brio. It also works with OBS, Xsplit, Zoom and Teams, so streamers can tune exposure directly. For anyone who does not want to fiddle, the MX Brio gets close with less work.

Buy it if you stream or record in a dim room and want to fix exposure and focus yourself. The caveat is time: manual controls mean more tuning, and it is not plug-and-play.

products.name: Elgato Facecam Pro, True 4K60 Webcam (Renewed)
products.verdict: The only true 4K at 60 frames per second here.
products.description:
The Facecam Pro records true 4K at 60 frames per second, with advanced light correction, DSLR-style manual controls and a wide-angle lens. It is the only 4K60 camera in this group. Sixty frames per second matters when you stream gameplay, demos or fast hand movement, because motion looks smoother than at 30.

It ranks third because this listing is a renewed unit in the $200 to $500 band. Refurbished stock carries warranty risk that new Logitech and Razer cameras avoid, and that offsets the frame rate advantage. It still leads the Logitech Brio on frame rate and manual control, but not on convenience.

Buy it if smooth motion is the priority and you accept renewed condition. The caveat is exactly that: confirm the seller's warranty and return terms before you order.

products.name: Logitech Brio Ultra 4K HD Webcam (Black)
products.verdict: True 4K that works with OBS, but needs USB 3.0.
products.description:
The Logitech Brio records true 4K with a wide field of view, auto-adjusting light correction and support for OBS and major streaming software. It needs a USB 3.0 port for full 4K, which is a spec many buyers overlook. On a USB 2.0 port the camera falls back to lower resolution.

It ranks fourth because the MX Brio offers USB-C and a privacy shutter in the same $100 to $200 band, and this listing shows neither a shutter nor the newer connector. For streamers who already own a USB 3.0 port, the gap is smaller, since both share the same core features.

Buy it if you have a USB 3.0 port and want true 4K with OBS support. The caveat is the missing shutter, so you will need a lens cover for privacy.

products.name: Logitech 4K PRO Magnetic Webcam for Apple Pro Display XDR
products.verdict: A magnetic 4K mount made for Apple Pro Display XDR.
products.description:
The Logitech 4K PRO is a compact 4K webcam with a magnetic mount designed for the Apple Pro Display XDR. The magnet gives stable mounting with no clip-on wobble, which clip cameras on thin display bezels often suffer from. It connects over USB and sits in the $50 to $100 band.

It ranks fifth because the mount fits one display, which narrows the audience dramatically. Few features are listed beyond 4K and the mount, so there is no shutter, manual control or frame rate detail to compare with the EMEET at a lower band. For its intended display, nothing here fits as cleanly.

Buy it only if you own the Pro Display XDR. The caveat is simple: on any other monitor it has no mount, so it is a poor general purchase.

products.name: EMEET C960 4K Webcam
products.verdict: The cheapest way to try 4K, with autofocus and dual mics.
products.description:
The EMEET C960 has a 4K UHD CMOS sensor, PDAF autofocus, dual omnidirectional microphones, a 73 degree field of view and a built-in privacy cover, all in the $25 to $50 band. PDAF autofocus refocuses faster than contrast-detect systems when you lean in or hold up an object.

It ranks last because the sensor is basic next to the Razer and its field of view is narrower than the wide-angle Logitech and Elgato cameras. But it costs a fraction of anything above and still has the shutter and mics that the Facecam Pro lacks.

Buy it if you are trying 4K for the first time. The caveat is light: a basic sensor struggles in dim rooms, so streamers who work at night should pay for the Kiyo Pro Ultra.

whatMatters.detail: Many video call apps compress your feed to 1080p or lower, so 4K matters mostly when you record or stream locally. If you only join meetings, a good 1080p camera looks identical and costs less. Decide your use first. For creators, 4K gives room to crop and reframe in editing without visible softness.

Frame rate is how many pictures the camera captures each second. 30fps looks natural for calls and talking heads, while 60fps looks smoother for movement and gameplay. Many webcams drop to 30fps at 4K. The Elgato Facecam Pro is the only camera here listed at 4K60. Check the frame rate at the resolution you plan to use.

A larger sensor gathers more light per pixel, which keeps footage clean in dim rooms. Auto light correction adjusts exposure when conditions change. The Razer Kiyo Pro Ultra lists a large sensor, while the EMEET C960 uses a basic 4K CMOS. Look for sensor size, not just megapixels, and check whether correction can be turned off.

Full 4K needs bandwidth. The Logitech Brio requires USB 3.0, and the MX Brio uses USB-C. On a slower port the camera drops to lower resolution without warning. Check what ports your computer has, and whether the cable supplied is the right type, before you buy. A hub can also cut bandwidth, so plug directly into the PC.

DSLR-style manual controls let you lock exposure, white balance and focus so footage stays consistent. The Razer Kiyo Pro Ultra and Elgato Facecam Pro list them. They help creators who light their own scene, but they add setup time. If you prefer plug-in and go, choose auto light correction. Check the control list in the listing.

faq.a: Often not. Zoom, Teams and similar apps commonly compress the feed to 1080p or lower. 4K matters when you record or stream locally with a camera like the MX Brio or Kiyo Pro Ultra.
The Logitech Brio needs USB 3.0 for full 4K, and the MX Brio uses USB-C. Plugging either into a USB 2.0 port will cap resolution, so confirm your computer's ports and use the supplied cable.
It can save money, but check the warranty. The Elgato Facecam Pro in this ranking is renewed, so verify seller terms and return policy. If you want fewer risks, the new MX Brio is easier to trust.

faq.q: How do I set it up?
faq.a: Plug the camera into a suitable USB port, install the maker's app if one is offered, and select the camera in your streaming or call software. The Razer Kiyo Pro Ultra and Facecam Pro reward a few minutes of exposure tuning.
Use a built-in shutter, like the one on the MX Brio, or a privacy cover, like the one on the EMEET C960. Cameras without a shutter, such as the Logitech Brio, need a separate lens cap.

faq.q: Does it work on a monitor mount?
faq.a: Most clip onto the top of a monitor. The Logitech 4K PRO is the exception, with a magnetic mount made for the Pro Display XDR, so it will not suit other monitors.

finalTake: Buy the Logitech MX Brio unless you have a specific reason not to: it handles calls and recording with the least setup. Streamers in dim rooms should pay for the Razer Kiyo Pro Ultra, and motion-heavy creators for the Elgato Facecam Pro. If 4K is only a curiosity, the EMEET C960 proves it cheaply.
